claims.text: Equimolar or nearly equimolar CoCrFeNiTi can exist as a homogeneous, single-phase solid solution with minimal chemical segregation or nanoscale ordering.
The simple solid-solution state of equimolar CoCrFeNiTi lacks coherent nanoscale precipitates or sufficient short-range order.
The absence of coherent nanoscale precipitates or sufficient short-range order leaves few effective dislocation-pinning sites.
Deformation of baseline CoCrFeNiTi is dominated by relatively easy dislocation glide.
Easy dislocation glide gives baseline CoCrFeNiTi high ductility.
Easy dislocation glide gives baseline CoCrFeNiTi good machinability.
Easy dislocation glide is responsible for the relatively low strength of baseline CoCrFeNiTi.
Easy dislocation glide is responsible for the relatively low hardness of baseline CoCrFeNiTi.
A slight composition change or tailored heat treatment can induce nanoscale ordering or coherent precipitates without causing extensive phase separation.
Coherent nanoscale precipitates or short-range-ordered clusters act as dislocation-pinning sites.
Induced nanoscale ordering or precipitates increase dislocation pinning.
Induced nanoscale ordering or precipitates should increase hardness and yield strength relative to untreated CoCrFeNiTi.
Induced nanoscale ordering or precipitates should increase compressive strength relative to untreated CoCrFeNiTi.
The strength increase caused by induced nanoscale features should be accompanied by a moderate decrease in ductility.
The changes in mechanical properties depend on the volume fraction and spatial distribution of the precipitates.
The proposed mechanism is limited to equimolar or nearly equimolar CoCrFeNiTi under room-temperature or moderately elevated-temperature quasi-static loading without additional phase transformations.
A baseline sample and an intervention-treated sample can be compared using microscopy, diffraction, hardness testing, and mechanical testing to relate nanoscale features to strength and ductility.
